title: The Deception of Demons and the Vulnerability of the Soul
english: Because the one who prays must be wholly separated from the things that imprint the mind. And you will inquire whether, as it stands with bodies and their thoughts, so it stands also with incorporeals and their logoi — and whether the mind will be imprinted in one way when it sees a mind, and disposed in another way when it sees its logos. From this we know how spiritual knowledge separates the mind from the notions that imprint it, and presents it unimprinted to God — because the notion of God is not in the imprinting ones; for God is not a body, but is rather in the non-imprinting notions.

Again, of the contemplations that do not imprint the mind, some signify the essence of incorporeals, and others their logoi; and it is not as it happens with bodies that it happens also with incorporeals: for with bodies, some imprinted the mind and some did not imprint it — but here, neither kind of notion imprints the mind.

Chapter 25. When the demon of gluttony, having struggled much and often, is unable to corrupt the imprinted temperance, then he plunges the mind into the desire for the most extreme asceticism — from which he also brings into the midst the things concerning Daniel, that poor life and the seeds (Dan 1:12), and recalls certain other recluses who lived thus throughout, or who began thus — and he compels [the monk] to become an imitator of these: so that, pursuing immoderate temperance, he may fail even of the due measure, the body not sufficing because of its own weakness — truly blessing with the body and cursing with the heart. I do not think it right to obey him in this, nor to abstain from bread and oil and water. For the brothers have thoroughly tested this most excellent diet — and this not unto satiety, and once a day. For I marvel whether anyone, being sated with bread and water, will be able to receive the crown of dispassion.

But by dispassion I mean not the cessation of sin in act — for this is called temperance — but that which cuts off the passionate thoughts in the mind, which the holy Paul also named the spiritual circumcision of the hidden Jew (Rom 2:29). But if anyone is disheartened by what has been said, let him remember the vessel of election, the Apostle, who finished the course in hunger and thirst (2 Tim 4:7). And the adversary of the truth, the demon of acedia, also imitates this demon, suggesting the most extreme withdrawal to the enduring one, calling him to the zeal of John the Baptist and of Antony, the first-fruits of the recluses — so that, unable to bear the long and inhuman withdrawal, he may flee in shame, abandoning the place — and he himself may then boast and say, ‘I prevailed against him.’

Chapter 26. The unclean thoughts admit matter for increase, and are extended along with many things; for they cross great seas in the mind, and do not decline to travel long roads, because of the great heat of the passion. But those purified in any measure are narrower than these, being unable to be extended along with things because of the weakness of the passion — whence they are also moved more contrary to nature — and, according to the wise Solomon, wandering outside for a time, they gather stubble for the unlawful brick-making (Exod 5:12), so that they may be saved like a gazelle from snares and like a bird from the trap (Prov 6:5). For it is easier to cleanse an impure soul than to call back to health again one that has been purified and wounded again, the demon of sorrow not permitting it, but always presenting to the pupils, at the time of prayer, the image of sin.

Chapter 27. The demons do not know our hearts, as some men suppose; for He alone is the knower of hearts, who knows the mind of men and formed their hearts one by one. But from the uttered word and such movements of the body, they know most of the movements in the heart — which I had wished to declare clearly now, but I was held back by...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Demonic interference during reading
english: a holy priest — who said it is unworthy for such things to be published and cast into the ears of the profane; for, he says, even the one who consorts with the adulterer becomes liable according to the law. Nevertheless, from such signs they know what is hidden in the heart, and from these they take occasions against us. Indeed, we have often reproved some who had reviled us, not being lovingly disposed toward them — wherefore we also fell to the demon of rancor, and immediately conceived evil thoughts against them, the same as we had formerly known to befall us.

Wherefore the Holy Spirit also rightly accuses us: ‘Sitting, you spoke against your brother, and against the son of your mother you laid a stumbling-block’ (Ps 50:20); ‘and you opened a door to the thoughts of rancor, and troubled the mind at the time of prayer, ever picturing the face of your enemy, and deifying him — for whatever the praying mind beholds, this it confesses worthy to be God.’ But let us flee, beloved, the sickness of backbiting; let us never remember anyone evilly, nor contort our faces at the memory of our neighbor.

For the evil demons scrutinize all our postures, and leave nothing against us unexamined — no reclining, no sitting, no standing, no word, no passing by, no glance; they scrutinize all, they disturb all, all day long they contrive craftiness against us, so that they may slander the humble mind at the time of prayer and extinguish its blessed light. Do you see what holy Paul also says to Titus? ‘In doctrine, an uncorrupt, sound, irreproachable word, so that the one from the opposite side may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us’ (Titus 2:8). And blessed David also prays, saying: ‘Deliver me from the slander of men’ (Ps 119:134) — calling the demons ‘men’ as well, because of the rational element of their nature. But the Savior also, in the Gospels, called ‘an enemy, a man’ the one who sowed among us the tares of evil (Matt 13:28). From him may we also be delivered by the grace of Christ our God, to whom honor and glory are due unto the ages. Amen.

Chapter 66. There are certain unclean demons who always sit beside those who are reading, and attempt to snatch away their minds, often taking occasions even from the divine Scriptures themselves and ending in evil thoughts. And sometimes, contrary to habit, they compel [them] to yawn, and impose a most heavy sleep, quite foreign to the usual — as some of the brothers supposed, by an ineffable natural contrariety; but I, having often observed, learned it to be thus: they touch the eyelids and the whole head, and chill it with their own body — for the bodies of the demons are exceedingly cold, and like crystal — whence we also feel the head being drawn as if by a cupping-glass, with a gnashing of the teeth. And they do this so that, drawing to themselves the heat stored up in the skull, the eyelids — slackened by the remaining moisture and cold — may overflow upon the pupils of the eyes. Indeed, I have often felt and found the eyelids hardened like crystal, and the whole face deadened and shivering. And yet natural sleep is by nature disposed to warm bodies, and renders the faces of the healthy blooming, as one may learn even from experience itself; but the unnatural and strained [yawnings] they bring about, thinning themselves and touching the inside of the mouth. But this I had not understood until today, although I have often suffered it; but I heard it from holy Macarius, who told me this and adduced as proof — according to an ineffable ancient tradition — the sealing of the mouth by those who yawn. And we suffer all these things because we do not attend soberly to our reading, nor remember that we are reading the holy oracles of the living God.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Recovery of the Soul and the Vision of the Divine Place
english: Chapter 67. Since there are also successions of demons — the first having grown weak in the war and being unable to stir the passion dear to him — observing these, we find it thus: when the thoughts of some passion become rare over a long time, and there comes a sudden boiling and movement of it — we having given no occasion through negligence — then we know that a harsher demon than the former has succeeded to us, and, keeping the place of the one who fled, has filled it up besides with his own wickedness. But this one also understands our soul very well, being warred upon much more violently than usual, and having suddenly fallen away from the thoughts of yesterday and the day before, with no pretext from outside intervening.

Let the mind, then, seeing these things, flee to the Lord, having received the helmet of salvation, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having drawn the sword of the spirit, and having lifted the shield of faith; let him say, looking up with tears to his own heaven: ‘O Lord Christ, power of my salvation, incline Your ear to me, hasten to deliver me. Become for me a defending God, and a place of refuge to save me’ (Ps 71:3). And let him especially polish the sword with fastings and vigils. For in seven whole days he will be afflicted, being warred upon and struck by the fiery darts of the Evil One (Eph 6:16); and after the seventh he will recognize him as gradually becoming like what has been taught, and remaining thereafter for a whole year — for the most part being wounded rather than wounding — until the one who succeeds him also arrives; if indeed, for a time, as with Job, we fall under them, and our houses are laid waste by the lawless.

Chapter 68. Unclean thoughts often admit matter for increase, and are extended along with many things. For they cross great seas in the mind, and do not refuse to travel long roads, because of the great heat of the passion. But those purified in any measure are narrower than these, being unable to be extended along with many things because of the weakness of the passion — whence they are also moved more contrary to nature — and, according to the wise Solomon, wandering outside for a time, they gather stubble for the unlawful brick-making, no longer receiving straw (Exod 5:7, 12). One must therefore keep the heart with all guarding (Prov 4:23), so that it may be saved like a gazelle from snares and like a bird from the trap (Prov 6:5). For it is easier to cleanse an impure soul than to call back to health again one that has been purified and wounded again, the demon of sorrow not permitting it, but always leaping upon the pupils of the eyes, and at the time of prayer presenting the image of sin.

Chapter 69. Christ raises the rational nature, put to death by vice, through the contemplation of all the ages; but His Father raises the dead soul — through the death of Christ — by the knowledge of Himself. And this is what was spoken by the Apostle: ‘If we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him’ (Rom 6:8).

Chapter 70. When the mind, having stripped off the old man, has put on the [new man] from grace, then it will also see its own state at the time of prayer, like sapphire or a heavenly color — which the Scripture calls the place of God, seen by the elders on Mount Sinai (Exod 24:10).

Chapter 71. The mind will not see the place of God within itself unless it has become higher than all things among things; and it will not become higher unless it has stripped off the passions that bind it through the notions to sensible things. And it will lay aside the passions through the virtues, and the bare thoughts through spiritual contemplation — and this [contemplation] again, when that light appears to it which, at the time of prayer, imprints the place of God.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
